title: Effects of acute cold and heat shocks on the protein profile of crayfish hemolymph
projectDescription: The aim of the present study was to investigate potential effects of low and high thermal shocks on the protein composition of hemolymph of marbled crayfish using quantitative proteomics. The results of the present study can provide insight into the mechanisms applied by decapod crustaceans to overcome high and low temperatures and may help the development of approaches to protect decapods in both natural habitats and artificial farms against thermal shocks, especially those imposed by ongoing climate change and global warming.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Experimental design The experiment consisted of three temperatures, including low (3 °C), control (24 °C) and high (32 °C). Animals were kept under related temperatures for 24 h. Each treatment group contained six animals. Incubators (Liebherr FK 5440, Austria) were used to create and maintain temperatures. All animals were kept under a 12-hour light and 12-hour dark photoperiod.  Protein Extraction and measurement  Hemolymph samples (n = 18, with six samples per treatment) were processed by dissolving them in 90 μl of lysis buffer composed of 1% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and 20 mM tris(hydroxymethyl)aminomethane (Tris) at pH 7.55. The hemolymph samples were homogenized on ice using a Branson Digital Sonifier® 250-D (Branson Ultrasonics Corporation, Danbury, USA) with a probe sonication method. The sonication was performed at 60% amplitude, consisting of five cycles of 5-second pulses on and 5-second pauses off. Following homogenization, samples were centrifuged using an Eppendorf benchtop centrifuge to eliminate cellular debris. The supernatant, which contained the extracted proteins, was collected, and protein measurement was performed using the Pierce BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany). Protein Digestion Protein processing began with reduction using 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) for 45 minutes at room temperature. This step was followed by alkylation with 40 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) for 45 minutes in darkness to prevent light-induced degradation. After alkylation, excess IAA was quenched by adding DTT to achieve a final concentration of 20 mM. A total of 50 µg of protein was used for hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) clean-up (ReSyn Biosciences, South Africa) and automated on-bead protein digestion, which was performed using a KingFisher Flex system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany) in a 96-well plate format, following established protocols[21]. The process began with the incubation of magnetic microspheres at a 1:10 protein-to-bead ratio. The beads were equilibrated using an equilibration buffer containing 15% acetonitrile (ACN) and 100 mM ammonium acetate (NH4Ac) at pH 4.5. Protein samples were added to a binding buffer (30% ACN, 200 mM NH4Ac, pH 4.5), which allowed protein binding to the HILIC beads. To eliminate non-specific proteins, the beads were washed twice with 95% ACN. The beads, now bound to the target proteins, were incubated with sequencing-grade trypsin (Promega AB) at a 20:1 protein-to-trypsin ratio in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate. This digestion step lasted 1 hour at 47°C. After digestion, peptides were extracted from the plate and dried using a SpeedVac (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany) before undergoing C18 desalting. Peptide desalting was carried out using BioPureSPN™ Mini PROTO 300 C18 columns (The Nest Group, Inc., MA, USA). Columns were pre-equilibrated with 100 µl of 70% ACN containing 5% formic acid (FA) and conditioned with 100 µl of 5% FA. Peptides were resuspended in 100 µl of 5% FA and loaded into the column. The column was washed with 100 µl of 5% FA to remove impurities. Elution of the cleaned peptides was performed with 100 µl of 50% ACN containing 5% FA. All centrifugation steps were conducted using an Eppendorf benchtop centrifuge at 50 × g for 2 minutes. Finally, the purified peptides were dried and stored at -20°C for later quantification and injection into the mass spectrometer. Mass Spectrometry Peptide digests were reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid (FA) and their concentration was determined using a NanoDrop 1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany). A total of 400 ng of peptides was injected into an EvoSep One LC system (EvoSep, Denmark) connected to a Q Exactive HF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany), which operated in positive ion mode for data-dependent acquisition (DDA). Peptide separation was carried out using a 15 cm fused silica capillary analytical column (75 µm x 16 cm Pico Tip Emitter, New Objective) packed in-house with ReproSil-Pur C18 material (1.9 µm particle size, Dr. Maisch GmbH, Germany). Separation was achieved using the 58-minute whisper method, which allows for efficient peptide elution prior to mass analysis. The mass spectrometer utilized a top-20 DDA method. MS1 scans were performed with a scan range of 375 to 1500 m/z, a target resolution of 120,000, an automatic gain control (AGC) target of 3 × 10⁶ ions, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. For MS/MS scans, ions with charges of 2 to 6 were selected for fragmentation using higher-energy collision-induced dissociation (HCD) with a normalized collision energy (NCE) of 27. Fragmented ions were analyzed at a resolution of 15,000 FWHM with an AGC target of 1 × 10⁵ ions, a maximum injection time of 20 ms, and an isolation window of 1.2 m/z.
dataProcessingProtocol: Mass spectrometry raw files were processed using MaxQuant (version 1.6.17.0; www.maxquant.org). The files were analyzed against two databases: Procambarus entries from UniProt (as of November 22, 2021) and the Procambarus virginalis P. pvirginalis_04 database[22]. The search parameters included carbamidomethylation of cysteines as a fixed modification, while oxidation of methionine and N-terminal acetylation of proteins were set as variable modifications. Default search settings were applied, including a precursor mass error tolerance of 4.5 ppm, a monoisotopic fragment mass error tolerance of 0.02 Da, and a 1% false discovery rate (FDR) for protein filtering. Protein intensity values obtained from the protein groups file were log2-transformed and normalized using NormalyzerDE[23]. Based on performance metrics and effectiveness in adjusting for systematic differences in protein abundance across samples, cyclic Loess normalization was selected as the preferred method[24] (Ballman et al., 2004; Smyth, 2005). The normalized, log2-transformed data were used for differential abundance analysis. The empirical Bayes moderated t-test (Limma)[25] was employed to compare protein abundance between control and clot hemolymph samples through the NormalyzerDE web interface. Proteins were considered differentially abundant if they met two criteria: a p-value below 0.05 and a fold change greater than 2.  Design and order of RAW files: 1T-6T: Cold shock, 7T-12T: Control, 13T-18T: Heat shock.
